items.label: Fill every bottle and jug — 4 L per person per day
Pack water purification (tablets, filter, or boil kit)
No-cook food: nuts, bars, tinned fish, dried fruit
Manual can opener + disposable cutlery
Infant, pet, and medical-diet supplies
Electrolyte sachets and a thermal flask
Cooler block frozen solid, charged power bank
Adhesive bandages, gauze rolls, medical tape
Antiseptic wipes and antibiotic ointment
Blister kit: moleskin, needle, alcohol swab
Pain relief: paracetamol and ibuprofen
7-day supply of personal medication
Tweezers, trauma shears, nitrile gloves
Printed dose chart for children
Emergency blanket and triangular bandage
IDs, cash, and a copy of insurance papers in a dry bag
Phone, charger, and a spare battery — all charged
Room passphrase written on paper (OffGrid recovery)
Headlamp, spare batteries, whistle, lighter
Local map marked with two rally points
Change of clothes, rain layer, spare footwear
Pet carrier, leash, food, and vaccination record
Keys — house, vehicle, shed — on one carabiner
Hub machine powered and on the same network
Every device joined the room (presence shows them)
Handheld radios charged, channel and privacy code noted
Meet points and a no-comms fallback time confirmed
Beacon presets tested: SOS, HELP, MAYDAY

sections.heading: Order of operations
sections.body: Filter first to remove sediment and cysts, then disinfect. Turbid water defeats chemical treatment — run it through cloth or a filter before dosing.

sections.heading: Boiling
sections.body: A rolling boil for one full minute kills bacteria, viruses and protozoa. At altitudes above 2000 m, extend to three minutes. Let it cool covered.

sections.heading: Chemical treatment
sections.body: Chlorine dioxide tablets: typically 30–60 minutes wait, follow the pack. Iodine is effective but avoid in pregnancy or thyroid conditions. Half-life drops with heat — never dose warm water.

sections.heading: Storage
sections.body: Re-contamination is the usual failure point. Keep treated water in a closed vessel, pour rather than dip, and date it after three days even when sealed.

sections.heading: Recognise it early
sections.body: The drift is subtle: uncontrollable shivering, clumsy hands, slurred speech, poor judgement. The moment coordination slips, stop and rewarm — decisions get dangerous here.

sections.heading: Rewarm correctly
sections.body: Remove wet layers, insulate from the ground, and add dry cover. Warm the torso core first — neck, armpits, groin. Avoid rubbing extremities; ice crystals in tissue do damage. Sweet warm drinks only if fully alert.

sections.heading: Do not
sections.body: No alcohol, no hard exercise to 'generate heat' once shivering stalls, no direct dry-heat on frozen skin. Severe cases (shivering stops, confused) need evacuation — handle gently; rough movement can trigger cardiac arrhythmia.

sections.heading: Three of anything
sections.body: Three fires in a triangle, three whistle blasts, three flashes — the universal distress pattern. Keep the pile ready: dry tinder, wind break, one match sequence you have practised.

sections.heading: Sound carries further than you think
sections.body: A whistle beats shouting by an order of magnitude and saves your breath. One long blast every minute, rest between. In the OffGrid beacon, use SOS at a slow 10–15 WPM so distant receivers can copy.

sections.heading: Make yourself contrast
sections.body: Bright fabric on open ground, mirror flashes toward aircraft (aim at the reflection patch, sweep across the target). Stay put once you have signalled — moving makes you invisible to a search that is already looking.
